questions.question: Could you replace the final `| otherwise = 0` in getSign with `| True = 0` and have it behave identically?
options: No — otherwise is reserved syntax that True cannot substitute for
Yes — otherwise is just an ordinary Bool binding equal to True, so a guard list ending in either one behaves exactly the same way
No — True can only appear as a value, never as a guard
Yes, but only in the very last guard position, never elsewhere
questions.explanation: otherwise = True in the Prelude, and any guard, anywhere in the list, is evaluated as an ordinary Boolean expression. Writing True directly instead of otherwise changes nothing about how the guard list behaves — only the readability of the source.
optionFeedback: otherwise is not a keyword or special syntax — it is a perfectly ordinary top-level binding, exactly as usable or replaceable as any other Bool-valued name.
Correct — since otherwise is defined as True, the two guards are indistinguishable to the compiler.
True is a completely ordinary Bool value and can appear as a guard anywhere a Boolean expression is expected, including here.

Nothing about otherwise's behaviour is special to the last position — it would behave as an always-succeeding guard wherever it was written, though placing it before other guards would make them unreachable, exactly as Pattern Matching's ordering rule warns.

questions.question: Why does a guarded equation write functionName parameters with no = sign on that first line, unlike an ordinary equation?
options: It is a typo that Haskell tolerates for historical reasons
Because the = sign belongs on each individual | line instead — the function's result is defined separately for each guarded case, not once for the whole equation
Guarded equations do not need an = anywhere because they never return a value
The = is optional and can be added or omitted freely
questions.explanation: In a guarded equation, each | condition = result line supplies its own result for its own case. There is no single right-hand side for the whole equation the way there is for functionName x = expression, so there is no single = to write on the header line.
optionFeedback: It is deliberate syntax, not a tolerated mistake — omitting the = on the header line is required, and including one there is an error (see the Common errors table below).
Guarded equations absolutely return a value — exactly one of the guarded results, whichever condition is first True.
The header line's = is specifically forbidden, not optional; each | line supplies its own required =

questions.question: With guards ordered score >= 70, score >= 80, score >= 90, otherwise (least restrictive first), what does grade 95 return, and why?
options: "A", because 95 satisfies score >= 90, which is the most accurate case
"C", because score >= 70 is the first guard listed and 95 >= 70 is True, so that guard wins before the later, more specific guards are ever checked
A run-time exception, because guards must be in ascending order
"F", because otherwise always matches first when guards are misordered
questions.explanation: Guards are checked strictly in the order written, and the first True guard wins immediately — the later, more specific guards (score >= 80, score >= 90) are never even evaluated once an earlier one succeeds. Since 95 >= 70 is True, "C" is returned even though 95 also satisfies the more specific conditions.
optionFeedback: "A" would only be returned if score >= 90 were checked and found True before any less-restrictive guard — but with this ordering, score >= 70 is checked first and already succeeds.
Guards do not have to be in any numeric order to compile or run; misordering causes wrong answers, not a crash.
otherwise is only reached if every earlier guard is False; here score >= 70 is True for 95, so otherwise is never reached at all.

questions.question: otherwise = True, and True is also just a plain Bool literal. Why not write | True = defaultResult instead of | otherwise = defaultResult — would it behave any differently?
options: It would behave identically, since otherwise is literally defined as True — the difference is purely readability, naming the intent "this is the catch-all case" rather than repeating a bare literal
| True = ... is a syntax error and cannot appear as a guard
otherwise evaluates lazily while True does not, so only otherwise is safe to use last
otherwise can only be used in the guards lesson, not in real programs
questions.explanation: otherwise is an ordinary Prelude name bound to the value True — there is no compiler magic involved. | True = defaultResult would compile and behave exactly the same way. otherwise is preferred purely for readability: it documents to a human reader that this guard is intentionally the always-true fallback, not an accident.
optionFeedback: | True = ... is entirely valid Haskell; True is an ordinary Bool value and can appear anywhere a guard condition can.
Both otherwise and True are simple, already-evaluated Bool values — there is no meaningful laziness distinction between them here.
otherwise is an ordinary Prelude binding available in every Haskell program, not something scoped to this lesson.

questions.question: In describe, why does the pattern (x:xs) need a guard at all, instead of just returning one fixed result for every non-empty list?
options: Because a pattern is only allowed to select an equation, not decide what result that equation returns

Because a non-empty list still needs its result to depend on more than just "is it empty or not" — whether it has exactly one element, and if not, whether its head is positive — and patterns alone can only express the list's shape, not those further conditions
Because Haskell requires every multi-equation function to use guards somewhere
Because null xs is not a valid expression to use inside a guard
questions.explanation: The pattern (x:xs) only tells Haskell "this list is non-empty, and here are its head and tail." It says nothing about whether the tail is itself empty, or what sign x has. Those are exactly the kind of range/compound conditions guards are for, which is why the pattern and the guards work together rather than either alone.
optionFeedback: A pattern does exactly this in every other function in this chapter — patterns select the equation whose body runs. describe's equation body just happens to be a guarded expression rather than a single result.
Correct — the pattern narrows to "non-empty list"; the guards then distinguish the further cases within that.
Plenty of functions in this chapter use no guards at all, e.g. axisOf and stW from the pattern-matching lesson — guards are not mandatory.
null xs is an ordinary Bool-valued expression, and any Bool-valued expression is valid as a guard condition.

questions.question: Calling describe [0, 9], which guard fires, and why does describe [] not get tried first?
options: describe [] is tried first for every call and always fails before the pattern-matched equation runs

describe (x:xs) is selected because [0, 9] is non-empty; among its guards, null xs fails (the tail [9] is not empty), so | x > 0 is tried next, and it fails too because x is 0, leaving otherwise to fire
The first guard, null xs, succeeds because x itself is 0
This call is rejected as non-exhaustive, since no case covers a list starting with 0
questions.explanation: Equation selection happens first, by pattern: [0, 9] matches (x:xs) with x = 0, xs = [9], not the [] pattern. Then, within that one equation, its guards are checked in order: null xs is False (xs is [9], not []), x > 0 is False (x is 0, not greater than 0), so otherwise supplies the result, "starts with zero or a negative".
optionFeedback: Equation selection tries patterns in order and commits to the first match; [0, 9] matches (x:xs) directly, not [] — describe [] never runs for this call.
Correct — pattern selects the equation, then its three guards are checked in order until one succeeds.
null xs checks whether the tail is empty, not whether x is 0 — for [0, 9], xs is [9], and null [9] is False.
(x:xs) matches [0, 9] perfectly well; there is no missing case here, and the otherwise guard supplies a defined answer.

questions.question: Why is where used for bmi in bmiTell, instead of writing weight / (height ^ 2) out again inside each of the four guards?
options: Writing it four times would be a syntax error
where computes bmi once and makes it visible to every guard and every result in the equation, avoiding both the repetition and the risk of the four copies drifting out of sync
Guards cannot contain arithmetic expressions directly, only names
where is required syntax whenever a function has more than one guard
questions.explanation: Repeating weight / (height ^ 2) in all four guards would work, but it is redundant and error-prone — if the formula ever needed to change, all four copies would need updating together. where names the shared calculation once, and because its scope covers the whole equation (every guard and every right-hand side), all four guards can refer to the same bmi.
optionFeedback: Repeating the expression would compile fine; the objection is about maintainability and repetition, not syntax validity.
Guards can absolutely contain full arithmetic expressions directly — bmiTell simply chooses not to, for the stated reason.
where is optional; a function can have several guards with no where clause at all (grade earlier in this lesson has no where).

questions.question: Could bmi have been defined with let ... in inside bmiTell instead of where, and still be visible to all four guards?
options: Yes, let and where are fully interchangeable in every position

No — a let binding's scope is the one expression it is attached to, and guards are evaluated before any single result expression is reached, so a let placed in a result would not be visible to the guards themselves
Yes, but only if let is placed above the function's type signature
No, because let cannot bind a Double value
questions.explanation: As the comparison table states, where's scope is the whole equation including every guard, while let ... in's scope is confined to one particular expression. Guards are conditions checked before any particular result expression runs, so there is no single result expression to attach a let to that would also reach the guards themselves. This is precisely why where, not let, is the natural choice when guards need to share a calculation.
optionFeedback: They are not interchangeable — their scopes differ in exactly the way that matters for this example, as the comparison table shows.
let's position is about which particular expression it attaches to, not about placement relative to a type signature — type signatures are unrelated to this scoping question.
let can bind any type, Double included; the limitation here is about scope (which guards can see it), not about what type of value it can hold.

questions.question: What precisely happens when a two-argument function name is wrapped in backticks, mechanically?
options: The function is redefined to accept its arguments in a different order

Nothing about the function itself changes; only the written position of its name moves from before both arguments to between them — elem x ys and x `elem` ys call the identical function on the identical arguments in the identical order
Backticks convert the function into a different, related function that does something similar
Backticks are required for every function call in Haskell, not just elem
questions.explanation: Backtick conversion is purely notational. elem x ys and x `elem` ys are two ways of writing one function application: same function, same two arguments, same order. Nothing about elem's definition or behaviour changes — only where you, the programmer, choose to write its name relative to its arguments.
optionFeedback: Argument order is unaffected — x `elem` ys still means "is x an element of ys", the same question elem x ys asks.
It is the same function, not a different one — compare the two ghci transcripts above, which give identical results for identical inputs.

Ordinary prefix application (name then arguments with spaces) is the default and by far the most common form; backticks are an optional, occasional notational choice for specific two-argument functions.

questions.question: Can any function be used with backtick notation, or only elem?
options: Only elem, because it is specially built into GHC for infix use
Any function that takes exactly two arguments can be written infix by surrounding its name with backticks — elem is simply a common, readable example
Only functions imported from Data.Char
Only functions whose name is a single word with no capital letters
questions.explanation: Backtick notation is a general Haskell feature: wrapping the name of any two-argument function in backticks lets you write it between its two arguments. elem `` is used here because `` c `elem` xs `` happens to read naturally in English, not because elem has special status.
optionFeedback: elem has no special compiler privilege here — the backtick mechanism works the same way for any two-argument function.
Data.Char has nothing to do with which functions support backtick notation; div, mod, and countless other two-argument functions from anywhere can be used the same way.
Naming rules for identifiers (lowercase start, etc.) are unrelated to whether a function supports backtick notation — any ordinary two-argument function qualifies.
